days.title: The Road of Life opens
days.imageCredit: A traffic controller beside a Lake Ladoga road sign on the ice road, winter 1941 to 1942. Still from Soviet film in The Battle of Russia (U.S. War Department, 1943), National Archives 111-OF-5, public domain. Tier: green.
days.post:
Many of the drivers on Leningrad's ice road steered standing on the running board, with the door hanging open, so they could jump clear if the ice gave way.

On 22 November 1941 the first motor convoy set out across frozen Lake Ladoga: 60 trucks led by Major V. A. Porchunov. Leningrad had been cut off by land since September, and the bread ration for everyone but workers was down to 125 grams a day, about three thin slices.

The ice was still thin. About 40 trucks went through it in the first week, and the toll tripled the week after.

Was sending trucks onto ice that thin a reckless gamble, or the only choice Leningrad had?
replies: It paid off. By the most common account the first run brought back 33 tons of flour. On 25 December 1941, with food coming across the lake, the ration went up for the first time, to 350 grams for workers and 200 for everyone else. By April 1942 the ice road had carried more than 350,000 tons into the city, and on the way back it carried people out: 554,186 civilians between 22 January and 15 April 1942 alone.

Photos: A traffic controller beside a Lake Ladoga road sign on the ice road, winter 1941 to 1942. Still from Soviet film in The Battle of Russia (U.S. War Department, 1943), National Archives 111-OF-5, public domain. On the card: Trucks on the Lake Ladoga ice road, winter 1941 to 1942. Photo by Yevgeny Khaldei, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

Sources: Road of Life and Siege of Leningrad, Wikipedia; Russia's Ice Road Truckers, HistoryNet; 360.ru; Parlamentskaya Gazeta; RIA Novosti; Encyclopedia.com; The Battle of Russia, National Archives.
days.alt: Archival film still of a Soviet traffic controller in a fur hat and heavy winter coat, arm raised, standing beside a signpost with Russian road signs pointing toward Lake Ladoga, bare winter trees behind him.
facts: 22 November 1941: the first motor convoy, 60 trucks under Major V. A. Porchunov, crosses the Lake Ladoga ice.
Leningrad had been cut off by land since September 1941; the frozen lake was its only link.
From 20 November the ration fell to 250 g for workers and 125 g, about three thin slices, for everyone else.
Most trucks were GAZ AA polutorkas, rated at a ton and a half; the first run brought back about 33 tons of flour.
About 40 trucks fell through the ice in the first week; the toll tripled the week after.
Hunger and cold killed about 100,000 people a month in January and February 1942.
The road carried more than 350,000 tons in, Nov 1941 to Apr 1942, and evacuated 554,186 civilians, 22 Jan to 15 Apr 1942.
Officially known as Military Road No. 101; it closed 21 April 1942 and ran again the next winter until 30 March 1943.

days.title: The flag over Strasbourg
days.imageCredit: Tanks of the French 2nd Armored Division come ashore in Normandy, August 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, National Archives 111-SC-192468, public domain. Tier: green.
days.post:
The radio message that told Leclerc his tanks were inside Strasbourg was four words of nonsense: "Tissu est dans iode." Tissue is in iodine.

At dawn on 23 November 1944 his French 2nd Armored Division drove on the city in several columns, guided by Alsatian resistance fighters. By mid morning three of the columns were stuck at the ring of forts. The column of Lt. Col. Rouvillois came in by an unexpected route through Schiltigheim, caught the defenders by surprise and drove its tanks to the cathedral.

Early that afternoon a spahi named Maurice Lebrun climbed the 142 m spire and fixed a French flag to it.

That flag kept an oath sworn in the Libyan desert in 1941. Is there a better kept promise in the whole war?
replies:
The oath went back to Kufra. In early 1941 Leclerc's Free French crossed the Sahara and besieged the Italian fort there, and the garrison surrendered on 1 March. The next day he had his men swear "not to lay down your arms until our colours, our beautiful colours, fly over the cathedral of Strasbourg."

The Germans still blew the Rhine bridge to Kehl before the French could take it. In January 1945, when Eisenhower weighed leaving the city undefended, de Gaulle called it a national disaster, and with Churchill's support Strasbourg was held.

Photos: Tanks of the French 2nd Armored Division come ashore in Normandy, August 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, National Archives 111-SC-192468, public domain. On the card: Gen. Philippe Leclerc lands in Normandy with the French 2nd Armored Division, August 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, National Archives 111-SC-192467, public domain.

Sources: Liberation and defence of Strasbourg, Chemins de memoire, French Ministry of the Armed Forces; Liberation of Strasbourg and Capture of Kufra, Wikipedia; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo of a Sherman tank rolling down the ramp of a landing ship's open bow doors into shallow surf, sailors standing inside the doors and a crowd of soldiers watching from the deck above.
facts: 23 November 1944: the French 2nd Armored Division under Gen. Philippe Leclerc liberates Strasbourg.
The division drove on the city at dawn in several columns, guided by Alsatian resistance fighters.
Three columns were stopped by the ring of forts; Lt. Col. Rouvillois's column got in through Schiltigheim.
Coded radio message: "Tissu est dans iode", tissue is in iodine, meaning they were inside.
Early afternoon: spahi Maurice Lebrun climbed the cathedral's 142 m spire and fixed an improvised French flag.
The Oath of Kufra, 2 March 1941, after the Free French took the Italian fort in Libya.
The Germans blew the Rhine bridge to Kehl before the French could take it.
January 1945: Eisenhower weighed leaving Strasbourg; de Gaulle, backed by Churchill, insisted it be held.

days.title: B-29s strike Tokyo from Saipan
days.imageCredit: Mount Fuji from the nose of a B-29 on the first raid on Tokyo since the Doolittle Raid, November 1944. Photo by Capt. Raymond Creekmore, National Archives 342-FH-3A03137-55663AC, public domain. Tier: green.
days.post:
111 B-29s set out to destroy one aircraft engine plant outside Tokyo. Only 24 of them bombed it.

On 24 November 1944 Brig. Gen. Emmett O'Donnell Jr. took off from Saipan at 06:15 in the B-29 Dauntless Dotty, leading the first raid on Tokyo since Doolittle in April 1942. The target was the Nakajima engine plant at Musashino.

Over Japan, at 27,000 to 33,000 feet, the bombers flew into winds of about 120 knots, the jet stream. Bombs blew off course and aiming became almost impossible. Seventeen planes turned back, 64 bombed docks and city areas instead, and strike photos found just 16 bomb bursts in the target area.

By March 1945 Curtis LeMay had the B-29s going in low, at night, with incendiaries. Was high altitude daylight bombing of Japan doomed from the start?
replies:
The enemy fighters were the smaller problem. The orders warned that 400 to 500 could rise to meet the bombers. The home islands had about 375, and about 125 came up. One Japanese pilot drove his damaged fighter into the tail of a B-29, which went into the sea off Honshu with everyone aboard. A second B-29 ran out of fuel and ditched, and its crew was rescued.

O'Donnell's copilot was Maj. Robert K. Morgan, who had flown the Memphis Belle over Europe. Dauntless Dotty was Morgan's own plane, named for his wife, Dorothy.

Photos: Mount Fuji from the nose of a B-29 on the first raid on Tokyo since the Doolittle Raid, November 1944. Photo by Capt. Raymond Creekmore, National Archives 342-FH-3A03137-55663AC, public domain. On the card: Brig. Gen. Emmett O'Donnell and crew under the nose of the B-29 Dauntless Dotty before a Tokyo mission, Saipan, November 1944. National Archives 342-FH-3A38987-A64263AC, public domain.

Sources: Craven and Cate, The Army Air Forces in World War II, Vol. V; Missions to Tokyo, Pacific Wrecks; HistoryOfWar.org; Dauntless Dotty, Wikipedia; Memphis Belle Memorial Association; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo taken through the framed glass nose of a B-29: snow capped Mount Fuji rises through the clouds below, with other B-29s flying in formation to the right.
facts: 24 November 1944: 111 B-29s from Saipan make the first raid on Tokyo since the Doolittle Raid of April 1942.
Leader: Brig. Gen. Emmett O'Donnell Jr. in Dauntless Dotty, off Isley Field at 06:15.
Copilot Maj. Robert K. Morgan had flown the Memphis Belle; the B-29 was named for his wife, Dorothy.
Target: the Nakajima aircraft engine plant at Musashino. The raid had been postponed from 17 November.
Winds of about 120 knots at 27,000 to 33,000 feet, the jet stream, threw the bombs off.
17 turned back; 24 bombed the plant, 64 hit docks and city areas; 16 bomb bursts in the target area.
Orders warned of 400 to 500 fighters; about 125 came up. One rammed a B-29, lost with all aboard.
Early 1945 LeMay replaced Hansell; in March the B-29s went in low, at night, with incendiaries.

days.title: Kamikazes hit four carriers
days.imageCredit: A kamikaze disintegrates in flames after hitting USS Intrepid off the Philippines, 25 November 1944. Official U.S. Navy photograph, collection of Fleet Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, NHHC NH 62958, public domain. Tier: green.
days.post:
The radar screens were full of American planes that day. That was the problem.

Around noon on 25 November 1944, Task Force 38's carriers were launching strikes on Luzon from about 160 miles east of Manila. With so many of their own aircraft coming home to land, the 5 inch guns could not pick out about a dozen Japanese planes coming in low and fast past the fighter patrol.

At 12:50 a Jill torpedo plane crashed onto USS Intrepid's flight deck, and eight minutes later a second plane hit her amidships. Essex and Cabot were struck the same afternoon, and burning wreckage fell on Hancock. Intrepid lost 69 men.

Halsey wrote that she "went through hell." Her fires were out within two hours, and she stayed on station.
replies:
Intrepid's fire marshal, Lt. Donald DiMarzo, led the fire parties on the hangar deck through the flames and explosions. He was killed fighting the fires and was awarded the Navy Cross after his death; his citation says he helped save his ship.

On Essex, a plane flown by Lt. Yoshinori Yamaguchi hit the port edge of the flight deck among aircraft fueled for takeoff, killing 15 and wounding 44. On Cabot, 62 men were killed or wounded, but she kept her place in formation.

Photos: A kamikaze disintegrates in flames after hitting USS Intrepid off the Philippines, 25 November 1944. Official U.S. Navy photograph, collection of Fleet Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, NHHC NH 62958, public domain. On the card: USS Intrepid burning after kamikaze hits, seen from USS New Jersey, 25 November 1944. National Archives 80-G-470268, public domain.

Sources: Antiaircraft Action Summary: Suicide Attacks, U.S. Fleet Headquarters, April 1945; USS Intrepid, USS Essex, USS Cabot and USS Hancock, Wikipedia; Intrepid Museum; DiMarzo's Navy Cross citation, Home of Heroes; Admiral Halsey's Story; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo of a huge burst of fire and black smoke above a carrier's deck edge as a kamikaze plane breaks apart, fragments flying across a gray sky, a gun mount and railing in the foreground.
facts: 25 November 1944, about 160 miles east of Manila: kamikazes hit Intrepid, Essex, Cabot and Hancock.
Radar was cluttered with returning American planes, so the 5 inch guns could not pick up the attackers in time.
Intrepid was hit at 12:50 and 12:58; 69 of her men were killed. Her fires were out within two hours.
Lt. Donald DiMarzo, Intrepid's fire marshal, was killed leading the fire parties; Navy Cross, posthumous.
Essex: hit by Lt. Yoshinori Yamaguchi's plane among fueled aircraft; 15 killed, 44 wounded.
Cabot: 62 killed or wounded, but she kept her place in formation.
Hancock's gunners blew apart a diving plane about 300 feet up; burning wreckage hit her deck.
Task Force 38 pulled back to Ulithi; Intrepid left for repairs on 26 Nov, reaching San Francisco on 20 Dec.

days.title: Six carriers slip out of the Kurils
days.imageCredit: Battleship Kirishima (left), the carrier Kaga and battleship Hiei in Hitokappu Bay, Kuril Islands, 23 November 1941, three days before the sortie. Imperial Japanese Navy photo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Tier: green.
days.post:
The diplomats were still talking when the carriers sailed.

On 26 November 1941, in Washington, Secretary of State Cordell Hull handed Japan's envoys the American terms. Among them: Japan must pull its forces out of China and Indochina.

That same day, at the top of Japan, six aircraft carriers weighed anchor in Hitokappu Bay in the Kuril Islands. Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, Shokaku and Zuikaku sailed under Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, with battleships, cruisers and destroyers around them, and steered east into the empty North Pacific.

Once those carriers left the bay, was there still any real chance of stopping what came next?
replies:
Not one of those ships would send a radio signal until the job was done. The photo above shows the carrier Kaga with the battleships Kirishima and Hiei, waiting in Hitokappu Bay three days before they sailed.

Campaign Series: Pearl Harbor · Day by Day · Day 1 of 12

Photos: Battleship Kirishima (left), the carrier Kaga and battleship Hiei in Hitokappu Bay, Kuril Islands, 23 November 1941, three days before the sortie. Imperial Japanese Navy photo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). On the series card: Zuikaku at Hitokappu Bay, November 1941, before the sortie. Japanese photo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons).

Sources: Pacific Wrecks; Pearl Harbor, Mises Institute; Wikimedia Commons.
days.alt: Archival photo of a wide, cold bay under snow covered hills, with a battleship at left and the flat topped carrier Kaga and another battleship at anchor in the distance.
facts: 26 November 1941: the Japanese carrier force leaves Hitokappu Bay in the Kuril Islands.
Six carriers: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, Shokaku and Zuikaku.
Commander: Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, with battleships, cruisers and destroyers as escort.
The force sailed under strict radio silence, course east into the North Pacific.
Same day in Washington, Cordell Hull handed Japan's envoys the American terms.
Among the terms: Japan must withdraw its forces from China and Indochina.

days.stamp: Campaign Series · Pearl Harbor · Day 2 of 12
days.title: Washington sends a war warning
days.imageCredit: Admiral Husband E. Kimmel, Commander in Chief of the U.S. Pacific Fleet. Office of War Information, National Archives 208-PU-108FF-1, public domain. Tier: green.
days.post:
The war warning sent to Hawaii named the places Japan was likely to strike. Hawaii was not one of them.

On 27 November 1941 Admiral Harold Stark, the Chief of Naval Operations, sent Admiral Husband Kimmel and the Asiatic Fleet a message that opened: "This despatch is to be considered a war warning." Talks with Japan had ceased, it said, and an aggressive move was expected within days, against the Philippines, Thailand's Kra Peninsula, or Borneo.

The Army sent its own warning to General Walter Short in Hawaii. He ordered an alert against sabotage.

Was the warning clear enough, or did naming those targets point Hawaii's eyes the wrong way?
replies:
Two warnings went out that day, one from the Navy and one from the Army. Kimmel, the man in the photo above, commanded the U.S. Pacific Fleet and received Stark's despatch. Short received the Army's, and his answer was an alert against sabotage.

Campaign Series: Pearl Harbor · Day by Day · Day 2 of 12

Photos: Admiral Husband E. Kimmel, Commander in Chief of the U.S. Pacific Fleet. Office of War Information, National Archives 208-PU-108FF-1, public domain. On the series card: Adm. Harold R. Stark, Chief of Naval Operations, April 1940. U.S. Navy, NHHC NH 49967, public domain.

Sources: the OPNAV war warning of 27 November 1941 and the Dorn Report, Pearl Harbor archive at ibiblio.
days.alt: Archival portrait of Admiral Husband E. Kimmel in a white uniform with shoulder boards and an officer's cap, standing on the deck of a warship with masts and rigging behind him.
facts: 27 November 1941: Adm. Harold Stark, Chief of Naval Operations, sends the war warning.
It opened: "This despatch is to be considered a war warning."
Sent to Adm. Husband Kimmel in Hawaii and to the Asiatic Fleet.
It said talks with Japan had ceased and an aggressive move was expected within days.
Likely targets named: the Philippines, Thailand's Kra Peninsula, or Borneo. Hawaii was not on the list.
The Army warned Gen. Walter Short, who ordered an alert against sabotage.

days.stamp: Campaign Series · Pearl Harbor · Day 3 of 12
days.title: Enterprise sails under war conditions
days.imageCredit: Peale Island, Wake, from the air, 25 May 1941, with Navy PBY patrol planes in the lagoon and a Pan American Clipper at the pier. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-451194, NHHC, public domain. Tier: green.
days.post:
Twelve Marine fighter pilots took off from Ewa thinking it was a training flight. They were really headed for Wake Island, nearly 2,500 miles west.

On 28 November 1941 the Wildcats of squadron VMF 211 landed aboard the carrier Enterprise, and Admiral William Halsey's task force sailed from Pearl Harbor to carry them to Wake.

Once clear of land, the captain issued Battle Order No. 1: "The Enterprise is now operating under war conditions." It closed with one plain line: "Steady nerves and stout hearts are needed now."

Was putting a carrier on war conditions that morning wise caution, or a dangerous gamble?
replies:
Within hours of leaving Ewa the pilots were aboard Enterprise, and Hawaii was falling behind them. The photo above shows part of where they were going: Peale Island at Wake, seen from the air in May 1941.

Campaign Series: Pearl Harbor · Day by Day · Day 3 of 12

Photos: Peale Island, Wake, from the air, 25 May 1941, with Navy PBY patrol planes in the lagoon and a Pan American Clipper at the pier. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-451194, NHHC, public domain. On the series card: USS Enterprise (CV 6) underway in the Pacific, June 1941. U.S. Navy photo, public domain.

Sources: Pacific Wrecks; Admiral Halsey's Story by William F. Halsey and J. Bryan III; Unto the Breach.
days.alt: Archival aerial photo of a low, flat island ringed by white beach and reef, with a long pier, a road across it and seaplanes anchored in the lagoon.
facts: 28 November 1941: Halsey's task force sails from Pearl Harbor with the carrier Enterprise.
Its job: carry the Wildcat fighters of Marine squadron VMF 211 to Wake Island, nearly 2,500 miles west.
The dozen Marine pilots took off from Ewa thinking it was a training flight.
Battle Order No. 1: "The Enterprise is now operating under war conditions."
It closed: "Steady nerves and stout hearts are needed now."
